solution:
**Heat** is energy in transit. It is the energy that flows between two bodies purely because they are at different temperatures, and it flows of its own accord from the hotter body to the colder one until the two reach thermal equilibrium. Being a form of energy, it is measured in joule (or in calorie), and how much of it a body contains depends on the body's mass, its material and its temperature.

**Temperature** is the property that decides the DIRECTION of that flow. It is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the atoms or molecules of the body, and it fixes the body's degree of hotness. It is measured in \(^\circ\)C, \(^\circ\)F or K, and it does not depend on how much of the substance is present.

The chapter's own summary puts it briefly: the temperature of a body determines its hotness, while heat energy is its heat content.

Two consequences worth remembering:

- A large tank of warm water at 40 \(^\circ\)C holds far more heat than a cup of boiling water at 100 \(^\circ\)C, yet heat still flows from the cup to the tank if they are joined, because flow follows the temperature difference and not the heat content.
- When two bodies are at the SAME temperature there is no net transfer of heat between them, however much heat each contains. This is the state of thermal equilibrium.

Calibrating a thermometer means fixing a scale on it, and it is done in three steps.

**1. Choose two fixed points.** A standard temperature interval is selected between two easily reproducible fixed temperatures — just as the metre is defined as the distance between two fixed marks. The fact that substances change state at fixed temperatures is what makes such reference temperatures reproducible. The two chosen are:

- the **ice point** — the melting point of ice, equivalently the freezing point of water;
- the **steam point** — the boiling point of water.

Both are taken at normal atmospheric pressure, because \(\S\)7.8 shows the boiling point shifts with pressure.

**2. Mark the thermometric property at each fixed point.** The thermometer is brought into thermal equilibrium first with melting ice and then with steam, and the value of its thermometric property — the length of the mercury column, the resistance of a wire, the pressure of a gas at constant volume — is recorded at each. Call these \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\).

**3. Sub-divide the interval.** The interval between the two marks is divided into equal parts, and each part is called one degree. The celsius scale uses 100 such divisions and the fahrenheit scale 180.

An unknown temperature is then read off by assuming the property varies linearly between the fixed points, which is Eq. (7.2) of the chapter:

\(T = \dfrac{100(P_{T} - P_{1})}{(P_{2} - P_{1})}\)

where \(P_{T}\) is the value of the property at the unknown temperature \(T\). This is exactly the calculation done in Examples 7.3 and 7.4, for a mercury column and for a resistance thermometer respectively.

Three scales of temperature are in common use.

**1. Celsius scale (\(^\circ\)C).** The ice point is marked 0 and the steam point 100, both at normal atmospheric pressure, and the interval is divided into 100 equal parts. Each division is one degree celsius.

**2. Fahrenheit scale (\(^\circ\)F).** The ice point is marked 32 and the steam point 212, again at normal atmospheric pressure, and the interval is divided into 180 equal parts. Each division is one degree fahrenheit.

**3. Kelvin or absolute scale (K).** Its zero is absolute zero, the temperature at which the pressure of an ideal gas would fall to zero. A kelvin is the same SIZE as a degree celsius, so the two scales differ only by a shift of the zero. This is the SI unit of temperature.

**Relation between them.** Because each scale is linear in the same physical quantity, the fraction of the ice-point-to-steam-point interval is the same on all three, which gives Eq. (7.3):

\(\dfrac{T_{C}}{100} = \dfrac{T_{F} - 32}{180} = \dfrac{T_{K} - 273.15}{100}\)

Two useful special cases follow at once:

\(T_{F} = \dfrac{9}{5}T_{C} + 32\) and \(T_{K} = T_{C} + 273.15\)

Note carefully that the 32 and the 273.15 are offsets of the ZERO of a scale. They cancel whenever a temperature DIFFERENCE is converted, so an interval transforms simply as \(\Delta T_{F} = \frac{9}{5}\Delta T_{C}\) and \(\Delta T_{K} = \Delta T_{C}\).

**Absolute zero is the lowest temperature that can be conceived — the temperature at which the pressure and the volume of an ideal gas would both fall to zero.** Its value is \(-273.15\ ^\circ\)C, and it is taken as the zero of the kelvin scale, so absolute zero is 0 K.

How it is arrived at: experiments on gases at low density show that at constant pressure the volume of a fixed mass of gas varies linearly with temperature measured in \(^\circ\)C, and that at constant volume the pressure does the same. Neither line can be followed indefinitely downwards, because a real gas liquefies first. But if the straight line is EXTRAPOLATED backwards — supposing the gas never liquefies — every such line, whatever the gas and whatever the quantity taken, meets the temperature axis at the same point, \(-273.15\ ^\circ\)C. That common intercept is absolute zero.

Two points worth noting:

- Because the temperature of a body is a measure of the average kinetic energy of its molecules, absolute zero corresponds to the state of minimum molecular motion. No temperature below it is possible, which is why the kelvin scale has no negative values.
- The size of one kelvin is the same as the size of one degree celsius; the two scales differ only in where the zero is placed.

The three coefficients are \(\alpha\) (linear), \(\beta\) (areal) and \(\gamma\) (cubical or volume) expansion. The relation between them follows from the fact that the SAME linear stretching produces all three.

**Relation between \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\).** Consider a square plate of side \(l_{0}\) at 0 \(^\circ\)C which becomes \(l_{T}\) at \(T\ ^\circ\)C. From Eq. (7.11), \(l_{T} = l_{0}(1 + \alpha T)\). Its area at 0 \(^\circ\)C is \(A_{0} = l_{0}^{2}\), and at \(T\ ^\circ\)C

\(A_{T} = l_{T}^{2} = l_{0}^{2}(1 + \alpha T)^{2} = A_{0}(1 + \alpha T)^{2}\)

But from Eq. (7.14), \(A_{T} = A_{0}(1 + \beta T)\). Equating the two,

\(A_{0}(1 + \alpha T)^{2} = A_{0}(1 + \beta T)\)

\(1 + 2\alpha T + \alpha^{2}T^{2} = 1 + \beta T\)

The values of \(\alpha\) are very small, of the order of \(10^{-5}\), so \(\alpha^{2}T^{2}\) is negligible against \(2\alpha T\) and may be dropped. Therefore

\(\boxed{\beta = 2\alpha}\)

**Relation between \(\gamma\) and \(\alpha\).** Consider a cube of side \(l_{0}\) at 0 \(^\circ\)C. Its volume at \(T\ ^\circ\)C is

\(V_{T} = l_{T}^{3} = l_{0}^{3}(1 + \alpha T)^{3} = V_{0}(1 + \alpha T)^{3}\)

and from Eq. (7.17), \(V_{T} = V_{0}(1 + \gamma T)\). Equating,

\(1 + 3\alpha T + 3\alpha^{2}T^{2} + \alpha^{3}T^{3} = 1 + \gamma T\)

Neglecting the terms in \(\alpha^{2}\) and \(\alpha^{3}\),

\(\boxed{\gamma = 3\alpha}\)

**Combining the two results:**

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\beta}{2} = \dfrac{\gamma}{3}\), that is \(\alpha : \beta : \gamma = 1 : 2 : 3\)

Both results are general, because any solid may be regarded as a collection of small squares (for the areal case) or of small cubes (for the volume case).

Thermal expansion has to be ALLOWED FOR in most engineering work, and in some cases it is put to use. The applications and precautions the chapter itself points to are:

**1. Gaps between rail sections.** A railway track is not laid as one continuous piece but in segments with small gaps between them, so that the rails have room to lengthen on a hot day instead of buckling. Exercise 3(vi) works out the size of such a gap.

**2. Sag in overhead transmission lines.** Metal wires for electrical transmission are strung with a deliberate sag. In summer they lengthen and the sag increases; in winter they contract, and had they been strung taut they would snap.

**3. Shrink fitting — mounting a ring on a wheel or an axle.** An iron ring made slightly smaller than the wooden rim it must grip is heated until it expands enough to slide over the rim, and then cooled, so that it contracts and grips tightly. The same method mounts a steel wheel on an axle. Exercise 3(vii) is exactly this calculation.

**4. Loosening a tight metal lid.** The metal lid of a glass bottle comes off easily when heated, because the metal expands more than the glass. For the same reason two metal vessels stuck together can be separated by heating the outer one.

**5. Liquid-in-glass thermometers.** The expansion of mercury or alcohol in a glass bulb is itself the thermometric property that makes the ordinary thermometer work.

**6. Allowance in bridges, pipelines and concrete roads.** Expansion joints are left so that the structure can lengthen in summer without cracking or buckling.

The anomalous expansion of water is a special case with its own consequences: because water expands on cooling from 4 \(^\circ\)C to 0 \(^\circ\)C, ice forms at the SURFACE of a lake and floats, and the water below stays liquid so that aquatic life survives the winter.

Because a gas, unlike a solid or a liquid, changes its volume and its pressure appreciably for even a small change in temperature — so the heat needed to raise its temperature by one degree depends on WHICH of the two is held fixed while the heating is done.

There are two natural ways to heat a gas:

**At constant volume.** The gas is confined so it cannot expand. It does no work on its surroundings, so every joule supplied goes into raising the internal energy, and hence the temperature, of the gas.

**At constant pressure.** The gas is free to expand as it warms. It therefore pushes back the surroundings and does work on them, and that work must be paid for out of the heat supplied. So ADDITIONAL heat is needed to achieve the same rise in temperature.

Hence

\(S_{p} > S_{v}\)

and a single number cannot describe the gas. Two principal specific heat capacities are therefore defined:

- \(S_{v}\), the principal specific heat capacity at constant volume — the quantity of heat absorbed or released for a rise or fall of temperature of unit mass of the gas through 1 K (or 1 \(^\circ\)C) when its VOLUME is kept constant;
- \(S_{p}\), the principal specific heat capacity at constant pressure — the same quantity when its PRESSURE is kept constant.

The corresponding molar quantities \(C_{v}\) and \(C_{p}\) are defined for one mole rather than unit mass, and are related to the principal values by \(C_{p} = M \times S_{p}\) and \(C_{v} = M \times S_{v}\), where \(M\) is the molecular weight. Table 7.4 of the chapter shows \(C_{p}\) exceeding \(C_{v}\) for every gas listed.

For a solid or a liquid the change in volume on heating is so small that the work done against the surroundings is negligible, which is why only one specific heat capacity needs to be quoted for those.

**Yes — for a given substance at a given pressure they are the same temperature. The two names describe the same point approached from opposite directions.**

The chapter defines this temperature as the one at which the solid and the liquid states of the substance are in thermal equilibrium with each other. At that temperature both states co-exist, and the temperature stays constant while the change of state is going on, because the heat supplied or removed is used to break or to form the bonds between the particles rather than to change their average kinetic energy.

The distinction is only in which way the change is running:

- **Melting point** describes the SOLID-to-LIQUID transition — the temperature at which a solid, on being heated, turns into a liquid.
- **Freezing point** describes the LIQUID-to-SOLID transition — the temperature at which a liquid, on being cooled, turns into a solid.

For water at one standard atmospheric pressure both are 0 \(^\circ\)C, or 32 \(^\circ\)F, as the chapter states.

**Two qualifications.**

1. The value depends on pressure. The melting point at one standard atmosphere is called the NORMAL melting point; the fusion curve \(l\)-\(s\) of the phase diagram (Fig. 7.10) shows how it shifts as the pressure changes. So the two points coincide only when compared at the same pressure.
2. The heat exchanged in the two directions is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign: melting 1 kg of ice ABSORBS the latent heat of fusion \(L_{f} = 3.33 \times 10^{5}\) J, and freezing 1 kg of water at 0 \(^\circ\)C RELEASES the same amount.

**(i) Sublimation.**

The change from the solid state directly to the vapour state, without passing through the liquid state, is called sublimation, and a substance which does this is said to sublime. During sublimation both the solid and the vapour states of the substance co-exist in thermal equilibrium.

Dry ice (solid CO\(_{2}\)), iodine and camphor are the standard examples. Most substances sublime only at very low pressures; carbon dioxide is unusual in subliming at atmospheric pressure, at a temperature as low as \(-78\ ^\circ\)C.

**(ii) Triple point.**

The temperature and pressure at which the fusion curve, the vapourisation curve and the sublimation curve of a substance all meet, so that its solid, liquid and gaseous states co-exist in equilibrium, is called the triple point of that substance.

It occurs at one unique temperature and one unique pressure for any given substance, which is what makes it valuable as a fixed point: the triple point of water is 273.16 K, and that is the reference temperature used in defining the kelvin and in the constant-volume gas thermometer of Example 7.7.

[Textbook note: this chapter quotes the triple-point PRESSURES as \(6.11 \times 10^{-3}\) Pa for water and \(5.1 \times 10^{-5}\) Pa for CO\(_{2}\). Both unit labels are misprints. The correct values are \(6.11 \times 10^{-3}\) atm (about 611 Pa) for water and about 5.1 atm for CO\(_{2}\) — and the book's own text half a page earlier gives the CO\(_{2}\) figure as 5.11 atm, contradicting the later number by roughly ten orders of magnitude. The TEMPERATURES quoted, 273.16 K for water and \(-56.6\ ^\circ\)C for CO\(_{2}\), are correct.]

Suppose one end of a metal rod is heated while the other end is kept cool. At first the heat arriving by conduction is partly used to warm each section of the rod itself, so the temperature of every section keeps rising. The rod is then said to be in the **variable temperature state**.

After some time each section stops warming: it is passing on exactly as much heat as it receives. The temperature at every cross-section of the rod is then CONSTANT IN TIME, though it is NOT the same from one section to the next — it still falls steadily from the hot end to the cold end. This condition is called the **steady state**.

So the steady state is the condition in which the temperature at each point of the conductor has become independent of time, no heat is any longer being absorbed by the rod itself, and all the heat entering the hot face passes through and leaves at the cold face.

Two things follow from it, and both matter for the rest of \(\S\)7.9.1:

1. Under steady state the temperature falls UNIFORMLY with distance from the hot end to the cold end. The fall of temperature per unit distance along the direction of heat flow is called the **temperature gradient**, \(\dfrac{T_{1} - T_{2}}{x}\).
2. The rate of flow of heat is the same across every cross-section. This is precisely the condition under which Eq. (7.34), \(Q = \dfrac{kA(T_{1} - T_{2})t}{x}\), holds, so the coefficient of thermal conductivity is always defined and measured in the steady state.

Note that the two ends reaching the SAME temperature is a different thing altogether; in principle that would take infinite time, and it is not what steady state means.

**Derivation.**

Consider a cube of side \(x\), each face of cross-sectional area \(A\), whose opposite faces are maintained at temperatures \(T_{1}\) and \(T_{2}\) with \(T_{1} > T_{2}\). Let steady state have been reached. Experiment shows that the quantity of heat \(Q\) that flows from the hot face to the cold face is

(i) directly proportional to the area of the face, \(Q \propto A\);

(ii) directly proportional to the temperature difference between the faces, \(Q \propto (T_{1} - T_{2})\);

(iii) directly proportional to the time \(t\) for which the heat flows, \(Q \propto t\);

(iv) inversely proportional to the perpendicular distance \(x\) between the two faces, \(Q \propto \dfrac{1}{x}\).

Combining the four,

\(Q \propto \dfrac{A(T_{1} - T_{2})t}{x}\)

\(\therefore Q = \dfrac{kA(T_{1} - T_{2})t}{x}\)   --- Eq. (7.34)

where \(k\) is the constant of proportionality, called the **coefficient of thermal conductivity**. Rearranging,

\(k = \dfrac{Qx}{A(T_{1} - T_{2})t}\)

**Definition.** Putting \(A = 1\) m\(^{2}\), \(x = 1\) m, \(T_{1} - T_{2} = 1\) K and \(t = 1\) s gives \(k = Q\). Hence the coefficient of thermal conductivity of a material is **the quantity of heat that flows in one second through unit area of a slab of unit thickness, when its opposite faces are maintained at a temperature difference of one degree, under steady state conditions.**

**Unit and dimensions.** The SI unit of \(k\) is J s\(^{-1}\) m\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\), that is W m\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\); its dimensional formula is \([\text{M}^{1}\text{L}^{1}\text{T}^{-3}\text{K}^{-1}]\). Its value depends only on the nature of the material — Table 7.7 lists 406 W m\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\) for silver against 0.024 for air, which is why metals feel cold to the touch and trapped air is such a good insulator.

Four everyday applications, each turning on the fact that some materials conduct heat readily and others hardly at all:

**1. Cooking utensils with insulated handles.** The body of a pan is made of a metal — aluminium, copper, steel — because metals have a high thermal conductivity and pass the heat of the flame quickly to the food. The HANDLE is made of wood, ebonite or plastic, all bad conductors, so that heat does not travel up it to the cook's hand.

**2. Thick walls, and hollow bricks, in cold storage rooms.** Brick is a bad conductor, so a thick brick wall greatly reduces the flow of heat from the warm surroundings into the cold room. Better insulation still is obtained with HOLLOW bricks, because the air trapped inside them is an even poorer conductor than the brick (Table 7.7 gives 0.8 for brick against 0.024 for air).

**3. Wrapping ice in a gunny bag.** To stop ice from melting it is wrapped in a gunny bag. The jute is itself a poor conductor, and the air filled in the interspaces of the sacking is a very bad conductor, so together they cut down the flow of heat from the warm surroundings into the ice.

**4. Insulated containers for cold drinks and ice-cream.** Thermocol, a very poor conductor, is used for the boxes in which cold drinks are carried on a picnic or ice-cream is brought home, so that heat from outside does not reach the contents.

Other examples that rest on the same idea: the double walls of a thermos flask with the space between them evacuated; woollen clothing, which keeps us warm because the air trapped between the fibres conducts heat away from the body very slowly; and the low thermal conductivity of glass, which is a DISADVANTAGE — hot water poured into a glass beaker expands the inner surface while the outer surface, not yet heated, does not expand, and the beaker cracks.

**Thermal resistance.** The opposition offered by a body to the flow of heat through it is called its thermal resistance, \(R_{T}\). The idea is introduced by analogy with electrical resistance: in an electrical conductor the ratio of the potential difference to the current, \(V/I\), is the resistance; here the ratio of the temperature difference across the body to the rate of flow of heat through it is the thermal resistance.

From Eq. (7.38),

\(R_{T} = \dfrac{T_{1} - T_{2}}{P_{\text{cond}}} = \dfrac{x}{kA}\)

where \(x\) is the thickness of the slab (or the length of the rod), \(A\) its cross-sectional area and \(k\) the coefficient of thermal conductivity of the material.

Two properties follow directly from that expression:

- The LOWER the thermal conductivity \(k\), the HIGHER the thermal resistance. A material with a high \(R_{T}\) is a poor thermal conductor and therefore a good thermal insulator.
- Thermal conductivity is a property of the MATERIAL alone, whereas thermal resistance is a property of the particular SLAB OR ROD — it depends on the material and also on the thickness and area of the piece. (The reciprocal of \(k\), which is a material property, is called the thermal resistivity \(\rho_{T}\).)

**SI unit.** \(R_{T}\) is a temperature difference divided by a power, so its SI unit is \(^\circ\)C s/J, equivalently K/W.

**Dimensions.** \([R_{T}] = \dfrac{[\text{K}]}{[\text{M}^{1}\text{L}^{2}\text{T}^{-3}]} = [\text{M}^{-1}\text{L}^{-2}\text{T}^{3}\text{K}^{1}]\)

[Textbook note: the chapter gives the unit as "\(^\circ\)C s/kcal or \(^\circ\)C s/J". Only the second of these is an SI unit — the kilocalorie is not an SI unit of energy — although the kcal form is still used in practice, and Exercise 3(xii) is set in it. The dimensional formula printed by the book is correct.]

Conduction and convection both need matter: conduction passes energy from molecule to molecule by collision, and convection carries it by the bodily movement of heated molecules. Radiation needs neither, because **the energy travels as electromagnetic waves, and an electromagnetic wave requires no material medium to propagate.**

The mechanism, as the chapter sets it out, is a two-fold process:

**1. Emission.** Every object possesses thermal energy on account of its temperature \(T\) (for any \(T > 0\) K). The rapidly moving molecules of a hot body emit electromagnetic waves, which travel with the velocity of light, \(3 \times 10^{8}\) m s\(^{-1}\). These are called thermal radiations. In this step the thermal energy of the hot body is CONVERTED into wave energy.

**2. Absorption.** These waves carry energy with them across the intervening space, whether that space contains matter or not. When they fall on a colder body they are absorbed by its slow-moving molecules, whose motion is thereby increased. In this step the wave energy is RE-CONVERTED into thermal energy, and the temperature of the cold body rises.

So heat is transferred by radiation without the intervening medium being heated at all, and without any need for a medium to be there.

**The standard evidence** is the Sun. The space between the Sun and the Earth's atmosphere is essentially a vacuum, yet the Earth receives large quantities of heat from the Sun. That heat can only have crossed empty space, so it cannot have come by conduction or convection.

Because transfer by radiation has the same properties as light, it is also the FASTEST of the three processes — conduction is slow, convection is rapid, but radiation travels at the speed of light.

**Statement.** Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of loss of heat, \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\), of a body is directly proportional to the difference in temperature \((T - T_{0})\) between the body and its surroundings, PROVIDED that difference is small.

\(\dfrac{dT}{dt} \propto (T - T_{0})\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{dT}{dt} = C(T - T_{0})\)   --- Eq. (7.39)

where \(C\) is a constant of proportionality, \(T\) is the temperature of the body and \(T_{0}\) that of the surroundings.

**Experimental verification.**

*Apparatus and procedure.* A calorimeter is filled up to about two-thirds of its capacity with boiling water and covered. A thermometer is fixed through a hole in the lid, its position adjusted so that the bulb is fully immersed in the water. The calorimeter vessel is kept in a constant-temperature enclosure, or simply in the open air, since room temperature will not change much during the experiment. The temperature on the thermometer is then noted at one-minute intervals until the temperature of the water has fallen by about 25 \(^\circ\)C.

*First graph — the cooling curve.* A graph of temperature \(T\) along the \(y\)-axis against time \(t\) along the \(x\)-axis is plotted. This is the cooling curve, Fig. 7.13 (a). It is seen at once that the curve is STEEPEST at the start and flattens as the water cools — that is, the rate of cooling is higher initially and decreases as the temperature of the water falls towards that of the surroundings. This is qualitatively what the law predicts.

*Second graph — the quantitative test.* Tangents are drawn to the cooling curve at several suitable points. The slope of each tangent, \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\), gives the rate of fall of temperature AT that temperature. These slopes are then plotted against the corresponding temperature difference \((T - T_{0})\), taking \((0,0)\) as the origin.

*Conclusion.* The second graph, Fig. 7.13 (b), comes out as a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. A straight line through the origin is exactly the statement that \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\) is directly proportional to \((T - T_{0})\), and its slope is the constant \(C\). Newton's law of cooling is thereby verified.

[Textbook note: the question asks about "thermal stress", a term this chapter never defines — its only two occurrences in the chapter's 28 pages are inside this question itself. The answer above therefore draws on the stress and Young's-modulus material of Ch.6 Mechanical Properties of Solids together with this chapter's own thermal-expansion examples, and says so, rather than presenting an outside concept as though the chapter had taught it.]

**Thermal stress.** When a body is heated or cooled it tends to expand or contract. If that change in dimension is PREVENTED — because the body is clamped, built into a rigid structure, or joined to another material that expands by a different amount — the body is put into a state of internal stress. The stress set up in a body on account of a prevented thermal expansion or contraction is called thermal stress.

If a rod of length \(l\) and coefficient of linear expansion \(\alpha\) is rigidly held so that it cannot lengthen when its temperature rises by \(\Delta T\), the strain it would have taken up freely is \(\dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \alpha\Delta T\), and by Hooke's law the stress developed is

thermal stress \(= Y \times \alpha\Delta T\)

where \(Y\) is Young's modulus of the material.

**An example of its disadvantages.** Pouring hot water into a thick glass beaker often cracks it. The inner surface of the glass is heated first and expands, while the outer surface — glass being a bad conductor, so that the heat does not reach it quickly — does not expand. The inner layer is therefore held back by the outer layer, thermal stress builds up between them, and because glass is brittle the beaker cracks.

Other everyday instances of the same trouble: a railway track laid without gaps buckles in summer, which is why the rails are laid in sections with gaps between them; concrete roads and long bridges crack unless expansion joints are provided; and a completely filled glass bottle bursts in a freezer, because water expands on freezing and the ice has nowhere to go.

[Note: the term 'thermal stress' is not defined anywhere in the text of this chapter — this exercise is the only place it appears. The definition above combines this chapter's treatment of thermal expansion with the ideas of stress, strain and Young's modulus from Chapter 6, Mechanical Properties of Solids. The examples are all ones this chapter itself describes.]

A thermal insulator is a material that does not let heat pass through it easily — that is, a material of LOW thermal conductivity \(k\) and correspondingly HIGH thermal resistance \(R_{T} = \dfrac{x}{kA}\). Since \(R_{T}\) is inversely proportional to \(k\), the poorer the conductor the better the insulator.

**Materials that can be used, and why:**

- **Trapped air** — the best of the common insulators, with \(k = 0.024\) J s\(^{-1}\) m\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\) at 0 \(^\circ\)C, some seventeen thousand times smaller than silver's 406. Air conducts heat very badly, and provided it is trapped in small pockets it cannot carry heat away by convection either. This is why hollow bricks insulate better than solid ones, why woollen clothes keep us warm, and why a gunny bag protects ice.
- **Wood, cork and paper** — poor conductors, used for the handles of cooking utensils and for packing.
- **Thermocol and plastic foams** — very poor conductors, and mostly trapped air by volume; used for containers that must keep ice-cream or cold drinks cold.
- **Wool, cotton and other fibres** — these work chiefly by holding air still between their fibres.
- **Glass, brick and concrete** — moderate insulators (\(k = 0.8\)), which is why thick brick walls are used for cold storage rooms.
- **Ebonite and rubber** — poor conductors, used where a handle or a grip must stay cool.

**The underlying reason.** In a solid, heat is conducted when molecules vibrating faster at the hot end pass their energy on to their neighbours by collision. In metals there are, in addition, free electrons which move through the material and carry energy with them very efficiently — which is why metals are good conductors of BOTH heat and electricity, and why, in general, a good conductor of heat is also a good conductor of electricity and a bad conductor of heat is also a bad conductor of electricity. Non-metals have no such free electrons, and gases have their molecules so far apart that collisions are infrequent; both therefore conduct heat poorly and make good insulators.

Given

\(V = 1 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^{3}\), \(T_{1} = 30\ ^\circ\)C, \(T_{2} = 100\ ^\circ\)C

\(\gamma_{\text{glass}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\) (\(^\circ\)C)\(^{-1}\), \(\gamma_{\text{liquid}} = 75 \times 10^{-5}\) (\(^\circ\)C)\(^{-1}\)

\(\Delta T = 100 - 30 = 70\ ^\circ\)C

Both the flask and the liquid expand. The liquid spills only by the amount by which its expansion EXCEEDS that of the flask holding it — this is the apparent expansion, and it is the same idea as Example 7.11.

Increase in volume of the flask

\(= \gamma_{\text{glass}} V \Delta T = 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 1 \times 10^{-4} \times 70 = 8.4 \times 10^{-8}\) m\(^{3}\)

Increase in volume of the liquid

\(= \gamma_{\text{liquid}} V \Delta T = 75 \times 10^{-5} \times 1 \times 10^{-4} \times 70 = 525 \times 10^{-8}\) m\(^{3}\)

Volume of liquid which overflows

\(= (\gamma_{\text{liquid}} - \gamma_{\text{glass}})V\Delta T\)

\(= (525 - 8.4) \times 10^{-8}\)

\(= 516.6 \times 10^{-8}\) m\(^{3}\)

\(\therefore\) the liquid that overflows is \(516.6 \times 10^{-8}\) m\(^{3}\), that is \(5.166 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^{3}\) or about 5.17 cm\(^{3}\).

Use the heat equation \(Q = m\,s\,\Delta T\) (Eq. 7.28) for each block and compare.

**Lead:** \(m = 2.0\) kg, \(s_{\text{lead}} = 128\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\), \(\Delta T = 30\) K

\(Q_{\text{lead}} = 2.0 \times 128 \times 30 = 7680\) J

**Copper:** \(m = 4.0\) kg, \(s_{\text{copper}} = 387\) J kg\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\), \(\Delta T = 5\) K

\(Q_{\text{copper}} = 4.0 \times 387 \times 5 = 7740\) J

Since \(7740\ \text{J} > 7680\ \text{J}\),

\(\therefore\) **heating the 4.0 kg block of copper by 5 K requires more energy**, by 60 J.

Note how close the two come. The lead has the larger temperature rise, by a factor of six, but copper's specific heat capacity is about three times lead's and its mass is twice as great — and \(3 \times 2 = 6\) almost exactly cancels that factor of six. The question is set to show that a comparison of this kind cannot be made on temperature rise alone: mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change all count equally in \(Q = ms\Delta T\).

Given

\(m = 5.0\) g \(= 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\) kg

\(L_{v} = 2.26 \times 10^{6}\) J/kg

The water is ALREADY at 100 \(^\circ\)C and the steam is required at 100 \(^\circ\)C, so no heat is needed to change the temperature — every joule supplied goes into the change of state. The heat required is therefore given by

\(Q = mL_{v}\)

\(= 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 2.26 \times 10^{6}\)

\(= 11.3 \times 10^{3}\) J

\(\therefore\) the energy needed is \(11.3 \times 10^{3}\) J, that is 11.3 kJ.

Note how large this is for so little water: raising the temperature of the same 5 g of water through the whole 100 \(^\circ\)C from freezing to boiling would take only \(5.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 4186 \times 100 \approx 2.1 \times 10^{3}\) J, about a fifth as much. It is this large latent heat of vaporisation that the chapter uses to explain why a burn from steam at 100 \(^\circ\)C is far more serious than a burn from boiling water at the same temperature.

Given

\(\left(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\right)_{1} = 0.05\ ^\circ\)C/s at \(T_{1} = 70\ ^\circ\)C

\(\left(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\right)_{2} = 0.025\ ^\circ\)C/s at \(T_{2} = 50\ ^\circ\)C

By Newton's law of cooling, Eq. (7.39), with \(T_{0}\) the temperature of the surroundings and \(C\) the constant of proportionality:

\(0.05 = C(70 - T_{0})\)   ...(1)

\(0.025 = C(50 - T_{0})\)   ...(2)

**Temperature of the surroundings.** Dividing (1) by (2) eliminates \(C\):

\(\dfrac{0.05}{0.025} = \dfrac{70 - T_{0}}{50 - T_{0}}\)

\(2 = \dfrac{70 - T_{0}}{50 - T_{0}}\)

\(2(50 - T_{0}) = 70 - T_{0}\)

\(100 - 2T_{0} = 70 - T_{0}\)

\(\therefore T_{0} = 30\ ^\circ\)C

**Constant of proportionality.** From (1),

\(C = \dfrac{0.05}{70 - 30} = \dfrac{0.05}{40} = 1.25 \times 10^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\)

**Rate of cooling at 40 \(^\circ\)C.**

\(\left(\dfrac{dT}{dt}\right)_{3} = C(40 - T_{0}) = 1.25 \times 10^{-3} \times (40 - 30)\)

\(= 0.0125\ ^\circ\)C/s

\(\therefore\) the surroundings are at 30 \(^\circ\)C and the rate of cooling at 40 \(^\circ\)C is 0.0125 \(^\circ\)C/s.

As a check, the excess temperature has fallen from 40 \(^\circ\)C to 10 \(^\circ\)C, a factor of four, and the rate of cooling has fallen from 0.05 to 0.0125 \(^\circ\)C/s, also a factor of four — which is the proportionality the law asserts, and the same conclusion Example 7.20 reaches.

At constant pressure the volume of a fixed mass of gas varies linearly with temperature, so a graph of \(V\) against \(T\) measured in \(^\circ\)C is a straight line (Fig. 7.2 (a)).

Experiments on gases at low density show that if this straight line is EXTRAPOLATED backwards to the temperature axis — that is, if we suppose, as the question asks us to, that the gas does not liquefy even at very low temperatures — the line meets the axis where the volume would be zero. The striking result is that the intercept is the SAME for every gas and for every quantity of gas: the lines for different gases have different slopes, but they all converge on one point.

That point is

\(T = -273.15\ ^\circ\text{C}\)

\(\therefore\) the volume of the gas would ideally be zero at \(-273.15\ ^\circ\)C.

This temperature is called **absolute zero**, and because it is common to all gases it is taken as the zero of the kelvin or absolute scale: \(-273.15\ ^\circ\text{C} = 0\) K. It is the lowest temperature that can be conceived, and no temperature below it is possible.

Two cautions. First, the result is an idealisation: every real gas liquefies, and then solidifies, long before this temperature is reached, so the straight line cannot in fact be followed all the way down. Second, absolute zero is unattainable in practice, however closely it may be approached.

Given

\(l = 10\) m (length of each rail section)

\(T_{1} = 27\ ^\circ\)C (temperature at which the rails are laid)

\(T_{2} = 45\ ^\circ\)C (maximum temperature in the region)

\(\alpha = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\) K\(^{-1}\)

The gap must be at least as large as the amount by which one rail section lengthens when it warms from the laying temperature to the maximum temperature. From Eq. (7.10),

\(\Delta l = l\,\alpha\,\Delta T\)

\(\Delta T = 45 - 27 = 18\ ^\circ\)C, and a temperature INTERVAL has the same size in \(^\circ\)C as in K, so \(\Delta T = 18\) K may be used directly with \(\alpha\) in K\(^{-1}\).

\(\Delta l = 10 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 18\)

\(= 216 \times 10^{-5}\) m

\(= 2.16 \times 10^{-3}\) m

\(\therefore\) the gap to be left is \(2.16 \times 10^{-3}\) m, that is **2.16 mm**.

If a smaller gap were left, the rails would press against each other on a hot day. Being unable to expand they would develop thermal stress, and the track would buckle sideways — which is exactly the danger the gaps exist to prevent.

Given

diameter of the wooden rim \(= 1.5\) m

diameter of the iron ring at 27 \(^\circ\)C, \(l_{1} = 1.47\) m

\(T_{1} = 27\ ^\circ\)C, \(\alpha_{\text{iron}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\) K\(^{-1}\)

The iron ring is made deliberately SMALLER than the wooden rim it must grip. It is heated until its diameter has grown to match the rim, slipped over it, and then allowed to cool, so that it contracts and holds the rim tightly. So we need the temperature at which the ring's diameter becomes \(l_{2} = 1.5\) m.

Every linear dimension of a body expands by the same fractional amount, so the DIAMETER of the ring obeys the linear-expansion relation just as a rod's length does. From Eq. (7.12),

\(\alpha = \dfrac{l_{2} - l_{1}}{l_{1}(T_{2} - T_{1})}\)

\(\therefore T_{2} - T_{1} = \dfrac{l_{2} - l_{1}}{l_{1}\alpha}\)

\(= \dfrac{1.5 - 1.47}{1.47 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-5}}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.03}{1.764 \times 10^{-5}}\)

\(= 1700.68\ ^\circ\)C

\(\therefore T_{2} = 27 + 1700.68 = 1727.68\ ^\circ\)C

\(\therefore\) the iron ring should be heated to about **1727.7 \(^\circ\)C**.

A remark on the answer: this is a very high temperature — iron melts at about 1535 \(^\circ\)C — so as a practical proposition the figures chosen in this question are unrealistic. A blacksmith in fact makes the ring only a millimetre or two undersize, not 3 cm, and then a few hundred degrees suffice. The calculation itself is the point of the exercise.

Given, on the scale X:

freezing point of water \(= 20\ ^\circ\)X (lower fixed point)

boiling point of water \(= 200\ ^\circ\)X (upper fixed point)

On the celsius scale the same two fixed points are 0 \(^\circ\)C and 100 \(^\circ\)C.

Any two linear temperature scales are related by taking the same FRACTION of the interval between their fixed points, which is the principle behind Eq. (7.3):

\(\dfrac{T_{X} - (\text{lower fixed point on X})}{(\text{upper}) - (\text{lower on X})} = \dfrac{T_{C} - 0}{100 - 0}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{T_{X} - 20}{200 - 20} = \dfrac{T_{C}}{100}\)

\(\dfrac{T_{X} - 20}{180} = \dfrac{T_{C}}{100}\)

For the liquid, \(T_{C} = 62\ ^\circ\)C:

\(T_{X} - 20 = \dfrac{180 \times 62}{100} = \dfrac{11160}{100} = 111.6\)

\(\therefore T_{X} = 20 + 111.6 = 131.6\ ^\circ\)X

\(\therefore\) the liquid boils at **131.6 \(^\circ\)X** on this scale.

Notice that the scale X has 180 divisions between the ice point and the steam point, exactly as the fahrenheit scale does, so an X degree is the same size as a fahrenheit degree; the two scales differ only in where the zero has been placed.

Given

\(T_{1} = 900\ ^\circ\)C. Convert to the absolute scale, since the gas laws hold only for absolute temperature:

\(T_{1} = 900 + 273.15 = 1173.15\) K

Let the initial pressure and volume be \(P_{1}\) and \(V_{1}\). Both are halved, so

\(P_{2} = \dfrac{P_{1}}{2}\), \(V_{2} = \dfrac{V_{1}}{2}\)

For a fixed mass of gas, Eq. (7.7) gives \(\dfrac{PV}{T} = \) constant, so

\(\dfrac{P_{1}V_{1}}{T_{1}} = \dfrac{P_{2}V_{2}}{T_{2}}\)

\(\therefore T_{2} = T_{1} \times \dfrac{P_{2}V_{2}}{P_{1}V_{1}} = T_{1} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{T_{1}}{4}\)

\(T_{2} = \dfrac{1173.15}{4}\)

\(= 293.2875\) K

\(\therefore\) the final temperature is **293.29 K**, which is about 20.14 \(^\circ\)C.

The essential step is the conversion to kelvin at the start. Had the calculation been done in \(^\circ\)C, quartering 900 would have given 225 \(^\circ\)C, which is wrong — the ratio \(PV/T\) is constant only when \(T\) is measured from absolute zero, not from the arbitrary zero of the celsius scale.

Given

\(\alpha_{\text{Al}} = 24.5 \times 10^{-6}\) /\(^\circ\)C, \(\alpha_{\text{Fe}} = 11.9 \times 10^{-6}\) /\(^\circ\)C

difference in length \(= 1.5\) m, and it is the SAME at all temperatures

Let the lengths at 0 \(^\circ\)C be \(l_{\text{Al}}\) and \(l_{\text{Fe}}\). At \(T\ ^\circ\)C, by Eq. (7.11),

\(l_{\text{Al}}(T) = l_{\text{Al}}(1 + \alpha_{\text{Al}}T)\) and \(l_{\text{Fe}}(T) = l_{\text{Fe}}(1 + \alpha_{\text{Fe}}T)\)

**The condition.** The difference between them is

\(l_{\text{Fe}}(T) - l_{\text{Al}}(T) = (l_{\text{Fe}} - l_{\text{Al}}) + (l_{\text{Fe}}\alpha_{\text{Fe}} - l_{\text{Al}}\alpha_{\text{Al}})T\)

For this to be independent of \(T\), the coefficient of \(T\) must vanish:

\(l_{\text{Fe}}\alpha_{\text{Fe}} = l_{\text{Al}}\alpha_{\text{Al}}\)   ...(1)

That is, the two rods must expand by equal ABSOLUTE amounts, so that the gap between them never changes. Since \(\alpha_{\text{Al}} > \alpha_{\text{Fe}}\), the iron rod must be the LONGER of the two, so

\(l_{\text{Fe}} - l_{\text{Al}} = 1.5\) m   ...(2)

**Solving.** From (1),

\(l_{\text{Fe}} = l_{\text{Al}} \times \dfrac{\alpha_{\text{Al}}}{\alpha_{\text{Fe}}} = l_{\text{Al}} \times \dfrac{24.5}{11.9} = 2.0588\,l_{\text{Al}}\)

Substituting in (2):

\(2.0588\,l_{\text{Al}} - l_{\text{Al}} = 1.5\)

\(1.0588\,l_{\text{Al}} = 1.5\)

\(\therefore l_{\text{Al}} = 1.417\) m

\(\therefore l_{\text{Fe}} = 1.417 + 1.5 = 2.917\) m

\(\therefore\) at 0 \(^\circ\)C the **aluminium rod is 1.417 m and the iron rod is 2.917 m** long.

Check: \(l_{\text{Al}}\alpha_{\text{Al}} = 1.417 \times 24.5 \times 10^{-6} = 3.471 \times 10^{-5}\) and \(l_{\text{Fe}}\alpha_{\text{Fe}} = 2.917 \times 11.9 \times 10^{-6} = 3.471 \times 10^{-5}\). The two are equal, so the difference in length is indeed unchanged by heating.

Given

\(Q = 50\) cal, \(m = 6\) kg

\(\Delta T = 62 - 20 = 42\ ^\circ\)C

From the heat equation, Eq. (7.28), \(Q = m\,s\,\Delta T\), so

\(s = \dfrac{Q}{m\,\Delta T}\)

\(= \dfrac{50}{6 \times 42}\)

\(= \dfrac{50}{252}\)

\(= 0.198\) cal/kg \(^\circ\)C

\(\therefore\) the specific heat of the metal is **0.198 cal/kg \(^\circ\)C**.

A note on the unit. Specific heat capacity is normally quoted per GRAM in the calorie system (water is 1 cal/g \(^\circ\)C) or per kilogram in SI. Here the mass has been given in kilogram while the heat is in calorie, so the answer comes out in cal/kg \(^\circ\)C, exactly as the question intends. Expressed in SI units it is \(0.198 \times 4.186 = 0.829\) J/kg \(^\circ\)C — a very small value compared with any entry in Table 7.3, which is a reminder that the figures in this question are chosen for arithmetical convenience rather than to describe a real metal.

[Textbook misprint: the printed answer's unit reads "°C s cal" with the solidus dropped. Thermal resistance is temperature difference per unit rate of heat flow, so the unit is °C s / cal. The value is correct.]

Given

temperature difference \(T_{1} - T_{2} = 30\ ^\circ\)C

rate of flow of heat \(P_{\text{cond}} = \dfrac{Q}{t} = 1500\) cal/s

Thermal resistance is defined, by analogy with electrical resistance, as the temperature difference divided by the rate of flow of heat. From Eq. (7.38),

\(R_{T} = \dfrac{T_{1} - T_{2}}{P_{\text{cond}}}\)

\(= \dfrac{30}{1500}\)

\(= 0.02\)

\(\therefore\) the thermal resistance of the copper rod is **0.02 \(^\circ\)C s/cal**.

Two points about this result. First, the answer is in \(^\circ\)C s/cal because the rate of flow was given in cal/s; in SI units it would be \(0.02/4.186 = 4.78 \times 10^{-3}\) K/W. Second, the value is small, as it should be for copper: \(R_{T} = \dfrac{x}{kA}\), and copper's thermal conductivity is one of the highest of any common material (385 J s\(^{-1}\) m\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\) in Table 7.7), so a copper rod offers very little opposition to the flow of heat. A good conductor always has a low thermal resistance, and a good insulator a high one.

[Textbook note: the printed answer is given as "0.02 \(^\circ\)C s cal". The solidus has been dropped in typesetting; the unit is \(^\circ\)C s per calorie. The numerical value 0.02 is correct.]

Given

time to heat the water from 0 \(^\circ\)C to 100 \(^\circ\)C, \(t_{1} = 20\) min

time to turn all the water at 100 \(^\circ\)C into steam, \(t_{2} = 90\) min

specific heat of water \(s = 1\) cal/g \(^\circ\)C

Let the mass of water be \(m\) grams and let the kettle deliver heat at a constant rate \(P\) — the same element is doing the work throughout, so this is the key assumption. Then the heat supplied in any interval is \(Q = Pt\).

**Stage 1 — heating the water.**

\(Q_{1} = m\,s\,\Delta T = m \times 1 \times (100 - 0) = 100m\) cal

and \(Q_{1} = P t_{1} = 20P\)

**Stage 2 — boiling the water away.**

\(Q_{2} = mL_{v}\)

and \(Q_{2} = P t_{2} = 90P\)

**Dividing.** Both \(P\) and \(m\) cancel, which is why neither is given:

\(\dfrac{Q_{2}}{Q_{1}} = \dfrac{mL_{v}}{100m} = \dfrac{90P}{20P}\)

\(\dfrac{L_{v}}{100} = \dfrac{90}{20} = 4.5\)

\(\therefore L_{v} = 450\) cal/g

\(\therefore\) the latent heat of vaporisation is **450 cal/g**.

A comment on the value: the accepted latent heat of vaporisation of water is about 540 cal/g (equivalently the \(22.6 \times 10^{5}\) J/kg of Table 7.6). The figure obtained here is lower because the assumption of constant power ignores the heat lost to the surroundings, which becomes appreciable during the long 90-minute boiling stage while the kettle sits at 100 \(^\circ\)C.

Given

\(x = 4\) cm \(= 4 \times 10^{-2}\) m

\(\dfrac{Q}{At} = 400\) kcal per minute per square metre

\(k_{\text{steel}} = 0.026\) kcal/m s K

**Convert the flux to per second**, since \(k\) is given per second:

\(\dfrac{Q}{At} = \dfrac{400}{60} = 6.667\) kcal/s m\(^{2}\)

From Eq. (7.34), \(Q = \dfrac{kA(T_{1} - T_{2})t}{x}\), so

\(\dfrac{Q}{At} = \dfrac{k(T_{1} - T_{2})}{x}\)

\(\therefore T_{1} - T_{2} = \dfrac{Q}{At} \times \dfrac{x}{k}\)

\(= 6.667 \times \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-2}}{0.026}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.2667}{0.026}\)

\(= 10.26\)

\(\therefore\) the temperature difference between the two sides of the plate is **10.26 \(^\circ\)C**, which is the same as 10.26 K.

The two units are interchangeable here because this is a temperature DIFFERENCE, and a kelvin is exactly the same size as a degree celsius — only the position of the zero differs between the two scales. That is why the printed answer quotes both.

[Textbook note (not an error): the printed answer of 10 minutes follows exactly when Newton's law of cooling is evaluated at each interval's INITIAL temperature, which is the only method this chapter uses — Example 7.20 applies \(\dfrac{dT}{dt} = C(T - T_{0})\) at a stated temperature and never introduces a mean-temperature refinement. Applying the law at the MEAN temperature of each interval gives 12 minutes, and exact integration gives 12.9 minutes. The solution above leads with the book's own method and then states the refinement, so a student who has met the integrated form is not left thinking one of the two is simply wrong. The stem also reads "How much time with it take" for "will it take".]

Given

First stage: cools from 80 \(^\circ\)C to 60 \(^\circ\)C in \(t_{1} = 6\) min

Second stage: cools from 60 \(^\circ\)C to 40 \(^\circ\)C in time \(t_{2} = ?\)

Room temperature \(T_{0} = 30\ ^\circ\)C

Both stages involve the same fall of 20 \(^\circ\)C, so the average rate of cooling in each is \(\dfrac{20}{t}\). Apply Newton's law of cooling in the form used in Example 7.20, taking the temperature at which each stage BEGINS as the temperature of the body:

**First stage**, starting at 80 \(^\circ\)C:

\(\dfrac{20}{6} = C(80 - 30) = 50C\)

\(\therefore C = \dfrac{20}{6 \times 50} = \dfrac{1}{15}\) per min

**Second stage**, starting at 60 \(^\circ\)C:

\(\dfrac{20}{t_{2}} = C(60 - 30) = \dfrac{1}{15} \times 30 = 2\)

\(\therefore t_{2} = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\) min

\(\therefore\) the sphere takes **10 minutes** to cool from 60 \(^\circ\)C to 40 \(^\circ\)C.

[Note on the method, worth reading: Newton's law gives the INSTANTANEOUS rate of cooling at a single temperature, and it holds only while the excess temperature is small. Applying it across a 20 \(^\circ\)C drop is therefore an approximation, and the answer depends on which temperature within the interval is used. The working above uses each stage's starting temperature and returns the book's 10 minutes. The more usual refinement takes the MEAN temperature of each stage — 70 \(^\circ\)C and 50 \(^\circ\)C — which gives \(C = \dfrac{20}{6 \times 40}\) and hence \(t_{2} = 12\) minutes; integrating the law exactly gives 12.9 minutes. All three are approximations to the same physics, and the difference between them is a measure of how far this problem stretches the small-difference condition the law requires.]
